utterances.text: I didn't ask you if you were aware of the command decisions. I was asking you whether you agreed that in all these circumstances we discussed, that was the only logical military choice to save the lives of your forces.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the way of thinking. I can't be the judge of that decision and say that that was the only option or perhaps there were other options as well. I can't say anything about that. Most probably that was the only option. Since we were outnumbered by the attackers, I would be prone to believe that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And the other thing that that did in the end of everything was it got thousands of Muslims completely out of the enclave with as few casualties to your forces as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise? I don't seem to understand your question. Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you are about to rephrase your question, Ms. Edgerton, I would even be inclined to give you 20 minutes for that, namely, during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'd lost track of the time, Your Honours. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, it's my task to keep an eye on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can assist as well, Your Honours. The document we used that has now been marked for identification at P7271 is already in evidence as P724, or at least a more complete version of the report with that first page is at that exhibit number, so that might assist Ms. Edgerton as he prepares the rest of her cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It assists all of us, Your Honours, and I'm grateful to Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which makes any objection moot therefore. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, I have to apologise. I offered you an opportunity to address us which I had forgotten about, which is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been asked by General Mladic to convey a piece of information. He has an appointment with the liaison officer with the International Criminal Tribunal and that appointment should take place about half past 1.00, and the General is kindly asking you to be able to leave the courtroom after the following break. He is agreeable that the examination of this witness is completed today in his absence, but the witness after that is very important to him, so he would kindly ask you not to start his testimony before he is able to return back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean that we would not start until Monday with the next witness because half past 1.00 until the end of the session, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's hereby clearly on the record that Mr. Mladic waives his right to attend court when we are concluding hearing the evidence of the present witness, but he does not waive his right to attend when the next witness will appear before this Court. Mr. Mladic -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you tell us - and I should have it somewhere - how much time you would need with Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I had asked for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll be very brief after we resume, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would suggest the following that we would start with the next witness, but if, Mr. Mladic, that we would stop at 1.30 or close to 1.30 and not continue to hear the evidence of the next witness in the absence of Mr. Mladic. He waives his right but if Ms. Edgerton needs only so little time, we could start with the next witness but we'll not continue once Mr. Mladic has left for his meeting. Another matter is -- but the meeting was with the liaison officer with the International Criminal Tribunal, liaison officer of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The liaison officer of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Trivun Jovicic. He is the liaison officer with the ICTY. And according to General Mladic, this meeting should take place between 1330 and 1400 hours in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what I do not fully understand why such meetings are planned at the time when Mr. Mladic is supposed to be in court. And, Mr. Stojanovic, I would urge you to try to find out whether that meeting could take place later today, or tomorrow, because the Chamber is not inclined to stop hearing evidence if -- without any consultation with the Chamber, meetings are planned during court time. I think it's the first time that it happens. So would you please try to find out whether that meeting could be postponed. If not, we'll consider what to do under the present circumstances. It's the first time that it happens, but certainly for the future, Mr. Mladic should not schedule any meetings with whomever at times when he is supposed to be in court. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not a meeting that was set by Mr. Mladic. This is the - a state official who is meeting all the detainees, and Mr. Mladic was scheduled by UNDU at that time. It's not a meeting that has been scheduled by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it was announced, then we'll certainly address the UNDU and tell that they should either change their schedule or -- I mean, the UNDU knows well when court hearings take place, and therefore they should have considered that when scheduling all this. And we'll address the Registry on the matter, and we'll try to find out whether any change can be made in today's schedule so that we don't have to unnecessarily lose time in court. We'll certainly address the matter when -- during the next break. The next break which will last until 20 minutes past --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to briefly address the matter which was raised by you, Mr. Stojanovic. First of all, the Chamber appreciates that Mr. Mladic took a position in which he waived his right and clearly distinguished between what is most important for him and what is still important but not that important that he would not allow us to continue. That's highly appreciated. Second, the information the Chamber received until now is the following: That it was not the UNDU which had determined that the meeting should take place within the court hours, but that the liaison officer had reported limited availability and today not until after the time which was finally then scheduled. The Chamber does not agree that the UNDU has agreed to such a meeting at a time when court is ongoing because however important those meetings may be - and the Chamber understands that this is, I would say, a routine meeting, there is not a special urgency in this meeting - that meetings should be scheduled when both parties to the meeting are available. Now, we do understand that the liaison officer has reported limited availability, but Mr. Mladic is, during court times, not available for such meetings if there's no urgent matter. Therefore, at this moment the Registry is seeking contact with the liaison officer in order to have this meeting postponed or rearranged during at any other time, and we would just continue in court as scheduled according to the court calendar. Then we perhaps already can invite the witness to be escorted into the courtroom again. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, meanwhile perhaps I can address your earlier inquiry about MFI P7171, about which you asked to be advised before the end of the day. That particular document has essentially been subsumed under larger discussions about demographics which have been ongoing between the Prosecution and Defence -- in fact, we anticipated further discussions about that today. But in light of the Court's inquiry, we can certainly take parallel steps to address this particular exhibit individually and hopefully come to a specific agreement, even before the larger discussions are concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When do you think we could hear from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll certainly be talking about that particular -- we can take the opportunity to talk about that particular document today, and hopefully we can have an answer for you by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me then set the time-limit by Wednesday so that some delay is already calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's when we would like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Micic. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So just to go back to that question that you were having a little trouble with, Mr. Micic, before we broke. It was about the effect of that corridor. So this Chamber's received evidence - and even from Mr. Borovcanin in the document we had a discussion about, P724 - that thousands of Muslim soldiers passed through that corridor while it was open. So you would agree with me, I take it then, that the effect of the corridor was that it got thousands of Muslims completely out of RS territory with as few casualties to Serb forces as possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: You can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then I have one last question. After the battles -- after the corridor closed, after the battles at Baljkovica took a different shape, your job with the 1st PJP Company was that you continued to comb the area that the column had come from to eliminate any remaining Muslim forces; right? That was your job.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that we combed the area, I can't remember that. I know that after the end of Baljkovica we returned to our stations, and we continued our regular police work in our police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your company, the 1st PJP Company, was kind of like the elite force of -- the elite company of the PJP, wasn't it? It was the fittest guys, the best-prepared guys; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're telling me now at the end of your testimony that the strike force of the PJP, after the corridor of Baljkovica closed -- or the corridor to let forces through to Nezuk closed on the 16th of July, just went back to Bratunac and hung around doing normal police duties?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: We did not hang around. We were assigned back to our original stations, where we performed our normal, regular police duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's just close by having another look at P724.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before we do that. Witness, you told us: "I don't remember that we combed the area. I can't remember that." And then you say: "I know that after the end of the Baljkovica was -- we returned to our stations." Now, if you don't remember whether you combed the area, if you immediately went back to your stations, then should we understand that as you did not comb the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember that I did that with my men. It doesn't have to apply to the entire unit, but I know that my men from Bratunac returned and continued performing their regular tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you said: "I know that after the end of the Baljkovica" you returned to your stations. Was there immediately after the corridor had been opened and immediately after any combat, or could it have been that "after the end" means that after the combat and after you had done some additional combing of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were not involved in the combing of the area, no way. As soon as combat ended, we returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So if we could -- oh, we've got P724 up on the screen in front of us. This is the report from Mr. Borovcanin that we looked at another version of earlier, Mr. Micic. Let's go, please, over to page 5 in both languages. Look at the entry dated 18 July 1995. It says: "A MUP combat group comprising the 2nd, 4th, and 5th Special Police Detachments and the 1st Company of the Zvornik PJP combed the areas of Cerska and Udrc ..." Are you saying that Mr. Borovcanin is lying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: No, no, he's not lying. I can't say that Borovcanin is lying. But I can't remember that, that's why I can't talk about any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you were ruling out, more or less, that you had been involved. Are you saying: I don't remember. It may have been the case? Or what is it? Are you positively saying: We were not involved? Or are you saying: We may have been involved but I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is this: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember everything, can I?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, this Court has received evidence that people were gunned down by -- in Cerska on the 18th of July by those forces that Borovcanin is talking about in this document. Your memory is faulty only because you don't want to implicate yourself. That's what's going on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN MICIC
utterances.text: No. I can't implicate myself. I had nothing to do with that. I'm not afraid. I can't -- I simply can't talk about I don't -- something I don't remember. If I told you I remember, then I would have to give you details. Borovcanin knows. If that's what he said, then he knows, and if the Trial Chamber has heard about that, then the Trial Chamber knows about that. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I just want to clear up something, Your Honour, to avoid -- to clear up a misstatement that I made. The evidence related to the 18th of July is not specific to the forces mentioned in that document, so I just want to be perfectly clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And actually I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Ms. Edgerton. Any further -- any re-examination by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I would just again thank the witness on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber also has no further questions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, may I take it that where a document was marked for identification earlier and where later Mr. Ivetic told us that it was already in evidence, that you wish to withdraw the tendering and that the number should be vacated?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, Your Honour. And my apologies. The descriptions were completely different, and it was our oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the number, Mr. Registrar, is vacated. Mr. Micic, apologies for dealing with administrative matters rather than addressing you. Mr. Micic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties and that were put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and all the best to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I received the -- a short message from the Detention Unit which explains briefly on how the scheduling of the appointment with Mr. Mladic took place, and I read the last line: "I have confirmed with Mr. Jovicic that he is content to await the return of Mr. Mladic from court, in order to ensure that they have their meeting without interfering with the proceedings." I therefore suggest that we'll just continue and that we have the next witness escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I would like to express the appreciation by this Chamber for the flexibility in rescheduling that meeting by the liaison officer. Mr. Registrar, I take it that this will be brought to the attention of the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pelemis, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, Mr. Pelemis. Mr. Pelemis, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I start, I'll need the help from the usher to distribute the statement summary to the court reporter and the booths, and one statement for the witness. You can give it to the Prosecution to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statements to the booths do not have to be -- only the statement which is given to the witness. If that's given to the witness then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if you would distribute that to the booth, yes. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon Mr. Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We speak the same language so I'll make a short pause after each of your answers for the benefit of the interpreters, so I don't want you to be confused if I wait a little after your answer. Would you kindly tell us your name and surname for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I am Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, have you given a statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement in Belgrade a year or two ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed it. This is the statement that I have given and I stand by it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the statement reflect accurately what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, it's all been recorded correctly. I have no comment and no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes. What I said in the statement is pure truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we have on our screens 1D1668, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the screen before you is the first page of a document. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, do you recognise the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the identical one, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender 1D1668 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D978, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read the statement summary of this witness and then I'll have several questions for him. With your leave, I would start with the statement summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Milorad Pelemis was commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in July 1995. Witness will testify on structure and functioning of 10th Sabotage Detachment, on its tasks and activities during relevant period, especially in July 1995 regarding operation in Srebrenica and upon its retrieval in Dragasevac. Witness was absent from his unit after the 12th of July, 1995, due to the injuries he sustained in the car accident on that day. He later found out that members of his unit were participating in liquidation of prisoners on Branjevo Farm on 16th of July, 1995. He will further testify on details regarding engagement of his unit in Srebrenica and individuals authorised to order usage of this unit. Mr. Pelemis will testify that no one from the hierarchical structure of the 10th Sabotage Detachment exercised command over this group or issued an assignment to these people on that day, namely on the 16th of July, 1995, meaning nor Petar Salapura, nor General Mladic, nor himself was in command of these people during executions on Branjevo Farm. And that was the end of the statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put any remaining questions to the witness as you announced --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, let us focus on the time just before the operation against Srebrenica. What orders did you receive before the operation and what orders did you issue, to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: If we are talking about the period starting the 1st of July, we were without any orders in Crna Rijeka defending the Main Staff. Then the forces from Srebrenica and Zepa attacked and came to the gate of the Main Staff. In the meantime, a group from the 10th Detachment -- Sabotage Detachment went on mission to Gradacac and reported to the Doboj intelligence centre. Another group of about 30 men was engaged in the defence of the Main Staff. We spent some time in combat together with the protection regiment and the units from Pijesak until the 4th of July. On 4 July, we received a few days of leave, but I received orders on the 6th of July to report to the Drina Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down slightly because the interpreters have to be able to follow you. Please proceed. You left off when you said: On the 4th of July, you received a few days of leave but you received orders on the 6th of July to report to the Drina Corps. Could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the 6th of July, I was resubordinated to the Drina Corps, and my mission was to carry out reconnaissance in the area of the Milici Brigade. In the planning of this operation, I involved about 20 men from the Vlasenica Platoon and we had ten men in Bijeljina in reserve. On the 6th of July, I reported to General Krstic, and he sent me to the Milici Brigade, to join that brigade, to carry out combat tasks in the western part of the area of the Milici Brigade around the hill called Buljim. Our mission was to take three bunkers from the defence line of the 28th Division and to mount a blocking defence until we are replaced by the Drina Corps. We spent two or three days there and there was obstruction from the people holding that part of the line. They didn't want to demine the minefield and they didn't want to co-operate. I did not manage in those couple of days to find the commander of the Milici Brigade, to speak to him, and on the 10th of July, in the early morning, Major Pecanac came to this area, Pribicevac. He brought me orders that I should go to the forward command post Pribicevac Srebrenica, and my task was to provide security of the IKM Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did Pecanac come? You speak so fast.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: He came to Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from Buljim you go where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I leave Buljim but I call another group from Bijeljina commanded by Franz Kos and the rest of the people from Vlasenica, from logistics, telling them to join us in Bratunac. They arrived at Bratunac around noon or 1.00 p.m., and then we went all together via Sase to Pribicevac. The unit was received by General Zivanovic and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was, what time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m. We couldn't have arrived earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exact date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: There I received directly from General Krstic in the presence of General Zivanovic to secure the command post in the broader area, which I did with those 30 men. And we spent that day in dug-outs that existed around the command post. And then for the first time, I saw fighting around Srebrenica because until then we knew nothing about it. On the 11th, in the morning, --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second. So that's the end of the 10th of July. What happens on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: In the morning, around 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning on the 11th, there was an attack by Muslims from Srebrenica, and they repelled our forces some way back. By 11.00 or 12.00, our forces remained -- managed to retake their positions. Generals Zivanovic and Krstic together give me the task to go to the area of the Zvornik Brigade to see Colonel Pandurevic, to get 30 men from him, and with that assault unit to enter Srebrenica and capture important features. I was against using that unit because it was not a unit meant to be used in assault, but Generals Zivanovic and Krstic persisted and said I had to execute that order. I had my doubts because I didn't want to advance and then to retreat and suffer losses, but they told me to just do as I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After receiving this order, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: We walked from Pribicevac to the feature called Bojna where the repeater was. That's about 2 kilometres from Srebrenica. There I met up with forces of the Zvornik Brigade and Colonel Pandurevic. I told him the corps command had ordered that my platoon -- in fact, my detachment and one platoon from his forces go to Srebrenica to take the command of the division, the municipal building, the courthouse, the communications centre, and the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After you said that to Pandurevic, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Pandurevic was also reluctant to go into the town, and then Pandurevic contacted Pribicevac with Pandurevic refusing to go into the town. However, after about an hour, he gave me a platoon commanded by a certain Mrga who got killed on the 16th or the 17th. About --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness stop and repeat how many men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't receive interpretation. The last thing we heard that the witness was -- the interpreters invited the witness to repeat the number he mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how many men set out in the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many groups did you form?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: The first thing I did was to tell all soldiers the rules of war. I banned them from burning anything in the town. I reminded them about the proper treatment of civilians. I told them that all the wounded and all the civilians should be gathered in the centre of Srebrenica at the school sports ground and that they would be taken over by the military police. The Zvornik platoon took that role and the capturing of various features was the task of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. So we set out immediately, and by the warehouse of the Red Cross we came across two or three women who were standing in the street. I introduced myself. At first, they didn't believe me. And then I asked one of them to go behind us and to inform people. I said nothing must happen to them, that I had given orders that they should all be gathered in the school sports grounds in the centre of Srebrenica. For their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The women that you encountered, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: They were Muslims. We could tell by their clothes and then in conversations with them. They were taken by surprise. We asked where their troops where and they said: Well, they were here a minute ago, they just ran by. They couldn't believe that the Serbian army was entering. Throughout the entire time, those women were helping us, they were inviting all the people on the right and the left side of the road to come out. And then when we took the last facility, which was the police station in Srebrenica, there were about 100 to 120 civilians walking behind us, women, children, and the elderly, and some five to six wounded people. Two or three were in uniform and two were in wheelchairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The civilians and the wounded, how far away were they from you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Some 50 to a hundred metres behind us, depending on the situation. We had our first skirmish in Petrica settlement near the mosque, and we had to find shelter in a canal together with the civilians. And after that, I ordered them to walk behind us at a distance of some hundred metres, that the lads from the Zvornik Detachment should keep them at a distance and make sure that nobody got killed during our fighting on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the way you had to engage in fighting. How many skirmishes were there? How often, how serious?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: The first somewhat stronger skirmish was in Petici [phoen] settlement near the mosque, and I suppose that some five to ten soldiers were there against us. The second was near Domovija Hotel where the command of the 28th Division was. And the third time we had to fight at the crossroads of the roads leading to Guber and to the centre. Our fourth skirmish was in the centre with two members. And then the last such resistance was put up -- or rather, they launched a counter-attack near the police station in Srebrenica. They had come from the left-hand side across the hilltop, and we suffered four wounded soldiers on that last occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which other men entered the town of Srebrenica together with you? Did everybody enter? Could you tell us something about the deployment of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: My unit was deployed in the following way. We immediately agreed that along the entire road we would leave a group of some three, four, or five men to comb the houses and other facilities and to provide security for the facilities of the 28th Division and the civilian authorities until the moment the civilian police and security organs arrived and took over their archives and documents. The second group under the command of Drazen Erdemovic assumed that task. The second section was taken over by the first group commanded by Franz Kos. The third group under the command of Lule Jokic took the court, the municipality, and the command of the brigade buildings. And the last group composed of myself and some four or five other lads stopped by the police station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, my microphone was off so nothing was recorded. The first group led by Franz Kos, where was it deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: At the section from the Catholic church to the crossroads of the roads leading to Guber on the one side and to the centre on the other side. The length of that section of the road was about 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Group 2?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Group 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Headed by Drazen Erdemovic, as you said it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes. Their position was from the Red Cross warehouse at the very entrance into Srebrenica to Cicevac settlement and the Catholic church there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long was that section that was guarded by Franz Kos's group and how far was it from the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Approximately 100 metres. That's how far his last soldier was from the city centre or from the town centre, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say the last one, do you mean the closest to the centre or the furthest away from the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: The closest to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Group 2, the closest soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: He was some 600 metres away from the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who was in the group that you led in the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: The entire road was already occupied and Lule Jokic gave me four man: Dragan Todorovic, Martic whose first name I don't know, Aleksandar whom we called Aco whose family name I can't recall, and Zoran Stupar. Four or five men all together, not more. And I took them over from Lule Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How close did Drazen Erdemovic get to the centre on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic remained in the second check-point near the mosque in Petric settlement. I believe that he was some 700 or 800 metres away from the centre. He never got any closer than that. On that occasion in a garage, in that part of the road, he found a Jugo car. He asked me if he could confiscate it and take it to Bijeljina. I said yes. As soon as we took the centre, Drazen Erdemovic got a task to go to Bojna feature and to report to our two men who were already there as members of the Zvornik Brigade, the driver and the communications man. He was also asked to use the radio communications means and let us know when General Mladic and others from the command entered Srebrenica and to explain to them that the road was free for them to use it. He actually did it immediately thereafter, so he did not spend a single minute in the centre. He never came even close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you do with the civilians, the wounded Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: They were behind us all that time. And in the centre where the flag of the 28th Division was, we already occupation the centre. Elements of the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades appeared, and I only know that I kept on communicating with a man who was around 28 years old and who lost all his fingers as a result of an explosion and he wore a camouflage uniform of the BiH army. He had a problem with some other lads from other units. I suppose that they recognised him. I told him to stand behind me and he managed to pass through, together with his mother, and arrived -- he arrived next to the police station. He was alive and well. I did not allow anybody to touch him. Moreover, there were two other wounded persons in wheelchairs. People from Bratunac recognised them as criminals, and I know that they accused them of having hanged two 12-year-old boys on a cross and sent them packing down the Drina River. I told everybody that nobody should touch them either. The other soldiers respected me. So those wounded people left in the direction of the playground together with all the other civilians, and later on they continued walking towards Potocari. They did not wait for the military police to turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned two men in the centre of the town. That conflict, that skirmish, with the two armed men in the centre, how was it? Can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm particularly keen to explain that because of Erdemovic, and I will tell you why. Erdemovic ascribed that incident to me, but I'll try and explain and tell you that Erdemovic could not have been an eye-witness of that incident. He may have heard that there had been problems, so in his own head, he construed the following story, or rather, he had the story in his head, whereas the truth is as follows. When we were in the centre of town and I was in the middle of a conversation with my lads, I told them to take the big flag of the 28th Division. All the forces that were on our flanks descended down to the centre. They started celebratory shooting into the air. There was some 200 or 300 people there, tops. They were celebrating their victory. At that moment, from a house on the side, two soldiers of the BiH army ran out. One of them went left and the other ran past us and continued running towards the police station. What I could observe was that he had a semi-automatic rifle in his right hand. I opened fire against him together with some two or three other lads from other units. Nobody hit him, everybody missed. And those soldiers joked at my expense and teased me that I was an officer and I still missed. Then we turned towards the group in the centre, and I could see that the other soldier had been hit and that he was lying next to the road. Some five to ten soldiers were approaching him to convince themselves that he was dead. He took the automatic rifle that they found on his body. I also have to say that as we were passing through from the beginning to the end to the moment when the town was taken or liberated, I observed four or five slain soldiers of the BiH army. Nobody had collected their bodies during the fighting. Erdemovic says that I ordered that. Impossible. Because later there was an investigation amongst ourselves, and we established that at that moment Erdemovic was at the Bojna feature, where he was waiting for the people from the staff and from the command in order to tell them that the road was free. He was standing next to the overturned transporters which was some 2 and a half kilometres from the place of the incident. I can also add to that, that according to him, I was either a lunatic or an idiot because he said that I -- because at the same time, I had about 120 people behind me who were civilians and wounded, and then all of a sudden it occurred to me to kill one soldier. First of all, I'm an officer. My word is my bond. I'm still in communication with the people in Srebrenica who know very well that I had done no harm to any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the time estimate was still on 30 minutes? Because you're now far closer to 40 than to 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously this time -- usually I ask for enough time, but today I'll need probably ten extra minutes. I apologise I didn't ask at the beginning for more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's take the break first and then I would like to keep you to those -- you said you'd need --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten more minutes. From the 30 or from now, the 40?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From now. We'll take a break. Ten minutes are granted, but then you are 20 minutes beyond the original 30-minute time estimate. The witness may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed and we'll carefully watch how the clock ticks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelemis, I would kindly ask you to keep your answers short because we have a lot of ground to cover. What was your relationship with Drazen Erdemovic? I know that this will take a bit longer to answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I knew -- I've known Drazen Erdemovic since 1991, when he was a member of the Guards Brigade in Belgrade, a professional soldier. He fought in Vukovar, and in 1994 when the 10th Sabotage Detachment was being established, he was among the ten Croats and Muslims who defected into territory of Republika Srpska and joined the Army of Republika Srpska. So he defected together with the others. Until the moment he signed his contract, and up until around March 1995, Erdemovic carried out all of his tasks. He was a good soldier. Thanks to his dedication and knowledge, he was promoted into sergeant. He signed that contract in February and he was Franz Kos's deputy. In March, some problems arose, he started drinking heavily. He was accused of some thefts around Bijeljina and all came to a head when sometime in November or December he sold his house to a refugee from Ilijas. He got 6.000 German marks. The man arrived with his wife and children the following day, but on that occasion Drazen Erdemovic and three other soldiers beat the man up. That man came to the barracks in Bijeljina to see me. He was with his wife and three children, and he complained about Erdemovic and his behaviour. Then I called Erdemovic and asked him to face the man in my office. The man immediately recognised him. I asked Erdemovic, "Do you have the money to return to the man?" He said, "No." And then I asked him, "Do you want me to give you a dead-line by which you're going to return the money to the man?" And he said, "No, I spent the money." Then I said, "As a human being, I have to help that man, he is a refugee from Sarajevo, he has no place to sleep, he paid fairly for the house which you cannot sell. Now you have to move out of your house, you have to move in with our friends and we have to confiscate your car that you used when you were wounded." After that he spread stories around the unit that he would pay me back, that he would retaliate. So all of our relations were good before March 1995, but then he started drinking. When he started drinking, he first ill-treated his wife and family and then he was involved in some threats and then he was involved in the shooting on the 22nd July. After that - and it is all well-documented - our relationship came to nothing. All of my attempts to somehow help him - because he was a family man - came to nothing. They were all in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness says "it's all well documented." Of course, in order to assess the reliability and the credibility of this evidence, the Chamber would appreciate if you either would address any documentation in relation to the wrong-doings of Mr. Erdemovic or -- so that -- I don't know whether you intend to do that, but -- such as name, selling the house, who it was, whether that is confirmed by the victim. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the name of that man?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: The man is still alive in Bijeljina. He has three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And his name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: His name is Ljubo and he is prepared to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some shooting on the 22nd of July. Who participated in that shooting in addition to Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Seven or eight other members were involved. On the 23rd, when I arrived in Bijeljina, when I had been invited to go there, I learned from the MUP that the previous night 53 bullets had been fired. The other participants were Zijad Zigic, Radislav Krmenovic, Stanko Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic and others. There were seven of them all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you approach the superior command and talk to them about Drazen Erdemovic at the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: At the end of 1995, I sent a letter to the superior command, asking them to talk to Drazen Erdemovic about his further stay in the unit because his behaviour undermined the reputation of the unit and he was no longer fit for the 10th Sabotage Detachment. I also asked them to send him for a psychiatric consultation because of his alcohol abuse; he was already an alcoholic by then. And already in the month of December he started spreading some stories about Zvornik, and I asked them to talk to him about that. I tried to take a statement from him but he didn't want to give it to him [as interpreted]. I asked him then to tell me about the circumstances of his participation in those things, and he flatly refused to give me any answers, and that's where my authorities ended. I referred all the documents to the superior command, and I left it to them to carry out further investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, because our time is up, what was your relationship with Boskic, good or bad?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Boskic was not an easy man to deal with. If you give him money, he will be your man. He can be bought. I have nothing nice to say about him. Of all the eight that signed the contract, he was one of the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And very briefly, we've already gone over our time. With your leave, I would ask you to explain about the 12th of July, the APC turned over and you were injured.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Around 4.00 p.m., as we were approaching the base in Dragasevac, there was a truck driving behind us and they tried to manoeuvre, to intimidate me probably, and then he grazed the APC, pushing it to the side. The APC fell down into a ditch 30, 40 metres below, in fact, it was not a ditch, it was a deep, and I blacked out. I woke up in the infirmary. I learned later that Koljivrat, Dragan was killed and Filipovic was lying next to me injured. Since the hospital in Vlasenica was full, they suggested to me that I continue my treatment in Sekovici. They gave me an ambulance and we set out around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. to Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: On the 12th of July. As we went back from Vlasenica, I asked the driver to stop by and I told the chief of logistics, Dragan Todorovic, that they are free to take leave until 17 July. The troops already knew that, but I asked him also to organise the funeral for Dragan Koljevic because he was a logistics man, it was his job. I continued on to Sekovici, to the hospital. In Sekovici, there is a document in the archives that I was received on the 12th of July, around 6.00 p.m., for treatment in the hospital of Sekovici. I stayed there until 19 July, when I was picked up by my brother from Belgrade, and he took me to Belgrade to his home, where I had further scans and X-rays and continued my treatment. The shooting in which those men were involved on the night of the 22nd forced me to get a car to pick me up from Bijeljina. I had to stop my medical examinations and treatment and go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Brano Gojkovic, what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: He was a private. He had no powers. He was not even a commander of a subgroup. He was quite a brave man but not very responsible. He was not fit for any great responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last question: Under normal circumstances, would he have been able to command Dragan Erdemovic or Franz Kos?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: In normal circumstances there was no way he could command Drazen Erdemovic or Franc Kos, because, first of all, he was a private, Drazen Erdemovic was a sergeant and Franz Kos was a second lieutenant or a lieutenant. Second, Gojkovic was in a platoon, support platoon, from Vlasenica, and the other two were from the sabotage platoon from Bijeljina. He could absolutely not command the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for their patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, do you acknowledge that Drazen Erdemovic and members of your unit summarily executed hundreds of Muslim men at the Branjevo Farm in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Yes, after these confessions in Sarajevo, yes, they were definitely involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you acknowledge that when Mr. Erdemovic pled guilty to his involvement publicly in January of 1996 of executing hundreds of men with your unit, that was a true plea, in that he -- excuse me, let me start over with that. When Erdemovic admitted in his guilty plea that he killed many hundreds of people, that was true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't believe it, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Now it's true, but the number of victims is a bit too much. In Sarajevo it has already been proved that it was no more than 200, but it's true that six men from my unit were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're wrong, sir. It's been proven in this court that it's been well over 8-, 900 people by DNA ID from the mass grave and the secondary mass graves. You're not aware of the evidence in this court, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I don't know exactly. I wasn't really so interested as to try to find out whether these -- I mean, what I really wanted to know, whether these six men were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you know Erdemovic testified that you issued the orders for them to go kill people so -- and you weren't interested?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I never issued that order to Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you must have known he blamed it on you when he pled guilty in 1996 and he testified at a Rule 61 hearing and laid it out in February of 1996. It's in this case at P1673. So tell us again, you weren't concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: First of all, I was not involved, and nobody from the structure of the 10th Sabotage Detachment was involved in the selection of men and their sending to that mission. What I know from Erdemovic's statement is that on the 16th, two officers from the Main Staff came to collect them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not invited to tell us what you're telling us now. The question was whether you really were not concerned about what Mr. Erdemovic said about you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Why would I be concerned when I was not present? Definitely, on the 16th, I was not in Dragasevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can be concerned if someone accuses you, even if it's a false accusation in your view, then people would usually be concerned about such accusations. That is, I think, what Mr. McCloskey is putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I came to testify here to remove that blemish from my name. I told you that Erdemovic when he was going to Serbia said that he would take revenge on me because I had taken his house and his car. And now in his statement he says also that only upon arriving at Branjevo he found out that they would be required to execute people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you on one thing, that you came here to testify to tell us what you know, not to remove any blame from yourself. You just answer the questions. And I urge the parties to ask about the facts. That's what you're here for. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a clarification to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you just told us you came here to remove the blame that he puts on you. That means, in fact, you are concerned even up to now about what Erdemovic said about you - is that correct? - that's why you're coming to clear your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Erdemovic made these allegations some -- over 18 years ago. This is the first time you have come out in any courtroom and said anything about this, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't give any statement to any police force about this, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I only gave a statement three years ago at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor in Sarajevo, and to them I made a statement about this event. That's all I have done from 1996 to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So years and years and trials and trials went on and on and Erdemovic testified in each one of them and said the same thing, and you didn't do anything until a few years ago?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: What could I have done? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Erdemovic gave a statement to the investigating judge in Belgrade in 1996, and he shortly after came here and pled guilty. Did you go to an investigating judge or did you go to the police in Belgrade and give a statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: No. I only asked the authorities if I should give a statement. They told me no because I had produced documents from the hospital that I was absent in that period. And from talking with other members of the detachment, I know that nobody had made allegations, nobody claimed that I was in Dragasevac on that day or that I had sent my men to Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you just testified that you were so concerned about the allegation he made to you on -- about you on the 11th of July that you had ordered the cutting of someone's throat that you had some kind of an internal -- you called it an investigation amongst yourselves. So did you have an investigation amongst yourself about the allegation he made on 11 July that you had a Muslim's throat cut?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to get a statement from all of them, from those six or seven who were at Branjevo, all of them refused. I'm trying to tell you that concerning the 11th, I am concerned. I want to tell you how badly Drazen Erdemovic was lying to you about that. He was many kilometres away from that place. I know that because there was a celebration going on at the time of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, as I mentioned, over 18 years ago he told that account of what happened in the centre of Srebrenica on 11 July, describing a person having their throat cut on your orders in the centre of town. And then many years after that, after many testimonies, we got a videotape, and there in the centre of town was a man lying in the road -- I'll show it to you. Let's take a look at it, P1147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's -- I'm thinking it's probably a good idea to give this man a 90(E) warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelemis, Mr. McCloskey invites me to give you a Rule 90(E) warning. Rule 90(E) says that if a truthful answer to any question that is put to you would tend to incriminate yourself, that you're relieved from -- you can address me and then ask to be relieved from the obligation to answer that question. We then, however, can compel you to answer the question but your testimony cannot be used against you, apart from any prosecution for perjury. So, therefore, if you feel that a truthful answer might incriminate yourself, you may address me. If that's clear to you, carefully listen to the next question put to you by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to show you a video-clip that was from 12 July from the centre of town, and it starts at 00.16.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So how was it, Mr. Pelemis, that many years after Erdemovic tells us someone has their throat cut on your orders that we find this man the day after where he said it happened with a fluid obviously coming down the road from his upper body? Did Erdemovic just get lucky with that? What's your explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I have said before that there were at least six such corpses lying around town as we were passing through. This man, as far as I can see, has a gun-shot wound in his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You see a gun-shot wound in his leg in this photo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a still so that the witness can explain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: He said "back," in his back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A gun-shot wound in his back. Could we scroll it back. Could you tell us, Witness, where you can see that there is a gun-shot wound in the back of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly in the middle of his back, as far as I'm able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've got some amazing vision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask a question. Would a gun-shot wound cause him to bleed like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may and doesn't have to. Depends on whether it cut through the artery and the man was bleeding out. I can't tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't look like the blood comes from the back. The jacket is clean at the back. It seems to come from underneath his neck.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the injuries on the front of his body are, whether it was from a shell, whether the chest was hit, I can't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, the evidence in this case from Mr. Erdemovic is, is that you told the troops before going into town not to hurt any civilians, and then when you came here in this area and this man came out looking for help, you had his throat cut by Zoran. Why on earth was -- did he need to die? Why did you order him to do that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I could not have ordered Zoran because Zoran was not there. And second, I never ordered anyone to do this. How do we then explain the 150 civilians and wounded walking behind me who did not miss a hair on their head? Why would I be concerned in a different way about this man? I repeat to you, there were five or six corpses that we saw while taking the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can get the reference, Zoran who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Erdemovic say, Zoran who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's just -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not here to answer his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the question is whether you are willing to clarify who in your question you refer to when you referred to an order to Zoran. If you're willing to do that, then we'd like to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know the Zoran with a nickname Maric?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD PELEMIS
utterances.text: I don't know Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's a good time to take a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn for the day, as a matter of fact, not only for the day but even for the weekend. Mr. Pelemis, we adjourn for the day. We will resume on the 30th, that's after the weekend on Monday, the 30th of March. We'd like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning, but before you leave this courtroom, I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given next week. If that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was waiting until this witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey, to give us the reference, because I couldn't find it, where Erdemovic said that killings had Branjevo Farm were ordered by Pelemis. Just a reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was about -- oh, perhaps yes. I leave it -- could you exchange this information which at this moment -- it may be important for the preparation of your cross-examination -- for -- of your re-examination, Mr. Lukic. And, therefore, Mr. McCloskey, I take it that you are willing to provide any reference Mr. Lukic is asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certainly, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that will be done. It doesn't have to be done in open court. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Monday, the 30th of March, 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.
